OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


THIS NRC STAFF DRAFT SE HAS BEEN PREPARED AND IS BEING RELEASED TO SUPPORT
INTERACTIONS WITH THE ACRS. THIS DRAFT SE HAS NOT BEEN SUBJECT TO FULL NRC
MANAGEMENT AND LEGAL REVIEWS AND APPROVALS, AND ITS CONTENTS SHOULD NOT
BE INTERPRETED AS OFFICIAL AGENCY POSITIONS.

13.       Research and Development

Chapter 13 of the Long Mott Generating Station (LMGS) preliminary safety analysis report
(PSAR) identifies those structures, systems, and components (SSCs) that require further
research and development (R&D) to confirm their design requirements. The PSAR states that
the R&D program is designed to resolve outstanding safety questions necessary to confirm the
adequacy of the design of certain SSCs prior to completion of construction of LMGS.

The applicable regulatory requirements for the evaluation of R&D are as follows:

      •    Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) 50.34(a)(8)

      •    Paragraph 50.35(a)(2) of 10 CFR

      •    Paragraph 50.35(a)(3) of 10 CFR

      •    Paragraph 50.35(b) of 10 CFR

      •    Paragraph 50.43(e) of 10 CFR

The NRC staff notes that while 10 CFR 50.43(e) is not applicable to a construction permit (CP)
application, completion of the R&D activities discussed in the PSAR may, in part, be necessary
for the required performance demonstrations at the operating license (OL) stage. As such, the
U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) staff considered the R&D activities in
contemplation of ensuring a clear path to demonstrating compliance with 10 CFR 50.43(e) at
the OL phase.

Applicable guidance on the NRC staff’s review of R&D activities includes:

      •    Division of Advanced Reactors and Non-Power Production and Utilization Facilities
           (DANU) interim staff guidance (ISG) DANU-ISG-2022-01, “Review of Risk-Informed,
           Technology-Inclusive Advanced Reactor Applications - Roadmap,” Appendix C
           (Agencywide Documents Access and Management System (ADAMS) Accession No.
           ML23277A139).

13.1.      Technical Evaluation

13.1.1. R&D Program Definition and Scope

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 13.2, which states that the scope of the LMGS R&D
program is determined based on an SSC demonstrating consistency with the following criteria:

      •    the subject activity must meet the 10 CFR 50.2 definition of R&D, and


                                                 13-1

                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION



   •   the subject SSC must fall within the established 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) scope of an R&D
       program by having an outstanding safety question that must be resolved to confirm the
       adequacy of the design by the completion of construction.

The PSAR further cites the definition of R&D from 10 CFR 50.2, “Definitions,” and states that
LME has not identified any SSCs or activities that would be appropriately characterized as
needing “research” to resolve outstanding safety questions tied to the construction of LMGS.
LME characterizes any such needs as “development” related. The PSAR defines ”research”
activities as “focused on experimental or theoretical work that may not have a defined use case”
and “development” activities as “apply the findings of previous investigative work to specific
testing needed to confirm the adequacy of the LMGS design,” consistent with 10 CFR 50.2.

Further, PSAR figure 13.2-1 lists being an SSC as a key criterion for inclusion in the R&D
program. As such, the PSAR narrows down the criteria for inclusion into the LMGS R&D
program to: 1) the subject activity meeting the 10 CFR 50.2 definition of R&D, 2) the subject of
the activity being an SSC, and 3) the subject SSC falling within the scope of an R&D program,
as described in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8).

While 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) focuses the scope of R&D on SSCs, the NRC staff’s view is that the
intent of 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8), in consideration of the definition of R&D in 10 CFR 50.2, is not to
limit R&D to only physical aspects of the SSC, but rather what is needed to understand the
SSCs and their functions to the level that the safety analysis can be confirmed to be valid, which
is the basis for the SSC classification, capability targets, and special treatment needed to set
design requirements impacting the physical SSCs. For example, the transient and safety
analysis methodology (TSAM) is a model used to represent the expected performance of the
physical SSCs within the facility during a transient event. If additional research is needed to
provide information to accurately model the safety-significant SSCs (e.g., reactor cavity cooling
system testing) this would be within the definition of 10 CFR 50.2 and the scope of 10 CFR
50.34(a)(8) and LME’s process for reviewing and updating the R&D program would result in
these SSCs being scoped into the R&D program.

The scope of the LMGS R&D program includes safety-related (SR) SSCs and non-safety-
related with special treatment (NSRST) SSCs that perform risk-significant functions but
excludes NSRST SSCs that are only required for defense-in-depth (DID) adequacy. The PSAR
states that this is appropriate because the NSRST SSCs relied upon for DID adequacy are not
required to prevent or mitigate any licensing basis event (LBE) from exceeding the frequency-
consequence (F-C) curve and do not provide a significant contribution to the cumulative risk
metrics selected for the total risk from all analyzed LBEs. While these statements accurately
align with the LMP SSC classification definitions in Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 18-04, LMP
also emphasizes the importance of maintaining adequate DID within the facility to ensure safety.
The NRC staff does not see any language in 10 CFR 50.2 or 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) that would
indicate an intent to exclude these SSCs from the scope of what is considered for R&D.

While the methodology used to scope activities and SSCs into LME’s R&D program appears
restrictive, the NRC staff confirmed in regulatory audit (MLXXXXXXXX) that testing or further
development needed to resolve safety aspects for activities and SSCs that are outside the
scope of the R&D program will still be performed as described in the PSAR and as needed to
support the OL application. LME indicated that the R&D program is a licensing program used to
track the activities and SSCs that LME has identified as falling into 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8). For

example, the full scope of the materials qualification, described in PSAR section 3.8, will be
performed under a program designed to ensure material aspects that could impact safety-
significant SSCs, are confirmed prior to the OL application. However, only those items related to
SR and risk-significant NSRST SSCs will be designated in the R&D program.

The PSAR further states that the R&D program will be reviewed and updated on an ongoing
basis and that SSCs may be added or removed from the LMGS R&D program: a) if the SSC
classifications are changed based on the PRA, and/or b) if the safety questions associated with
an R&D item are either identified or eliminated as part of the ongoing updates. The PSAR states
that for items in the R&D program where safety questions are resolved, the activities will be
marked complete in the R&D program.

As captured in RCI-1 (ML26239A157) and confirmed by LME, additional risk-significance
evaluations performed indicate that multiple systems currently classified as NSRST for DID may
be re-classified as risk-significant NSRST. Based on the methodology defined in PSAR
chapter 13, these SSCs will be re-evaluated by LME for inclusion in the R&D program when
changes to the safety classification or risk-significance occur.

13.1.2. SSCs in the LMGS R&D Program

This section presents the NRC staff’s evaluation of the items identified by LME as within the
R&D program.

Graphite Core Assembly

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 13.3.1, which indicates that uncertainties exist around
the performance of Graphite material in the Xe-100 operating environment. The Xe-100
operating environment is expected to be a high fluence, high temperature, and oxidizing
environment. The uncertainties are primarily due to limitations of existing codes and standards.
Therefore, LME included the graphite core assembly (GCA) in its R&D program to resolve
outstanding questions regarding the GCA’s performance in a high fluence, high temperature,
and oxidizing environment which can potentially impact its ability to perform its required safety
functions (RSFs).

The PSAR states that R&D testing is described in detail in “Xe-100 Licensing Topical Report
Graphite Core Assembly Material Qualification and Design Methodologies, Revision 2”
(ML26114A162, incorporated by reference) and that any outstanding safety questions will be
addressed prior to completion of construction of LMGS. PSAR table 1.4-14 lists the limitations
and conditions (L&Cs) associated with use of the Licensing Topical Report (LTR) along with
LME’s proposed plan to meet each condition as part of the R&D program. The acceptability of
LME’s proposed plan to address L&Cs associated with the use of GCA LTR as part of R&D
program is discussed in section 1.3.4 of this SE.

Because further testing performed for the GCA in a prototypic Xe-100 operating environment
would reasonably resolve the safety questions related to its performance in a high fluence, high
temperature, and oxidizing environment, and because the work will be completed prior to the
completion of construction, the NRC staff determined that the R&D activities planned for GCA
are consistent with the requirements of 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) and 10 CFR 50.35(a)(3).

Safety-Related Metallic SSCs

                                              13-3

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION



The NRC staff reviewed PSAR table 13.3.2-1, which lists the metallic assessments, testing, and
analysis and the affected SR metallic SSCs that are included in the R&D program. PSAR
section 13.3.2 indicates that uncertainties exist around the performance of metallic materials of
these SSCs in the Xe-100 operating environment primarily due to limitations of existing codes
and standards. The PSAR states that no additional code and environmental assessments tied to
SR SSCs, beyond those listed in PSAR table 13.3.2-1, have been identified as necessary for
the preliminary design.

The PSAR states that R&D testing is described in detail in the LMGS material qualification plan
and any outstanding safety questions identified will be addressed prior to the completion of the
construction of LMGS. The acceptability of the LMGS material qualification plan is discussed in
section 3.8 of this SE. As confirmed by the NRC staff in RCI-1 (ML26239A157), LME is in the
process of incorporating the results of updated risk-significance evaluations following the
NEI 18-04 methodology. As stated in PSAR section 13.3.2, SR and risk significant NSRST
SSCs may be added to the R&D program based on the changes in classification. For the SSCs
that elevate to risk-significant based on the evaluation described in RCI-1, and have outstanding
safety questions to be addressed, the SSCs would be added to the R&D program based on the
LME methodology.

Because LME’s planned testing for the SR metallic SSCs is in a prototypic Xe-100 operating
environment (i.e., high fluence, high temperature, and oxidizing environment), the NRC staff
determined that the planned testing will reasonably resolve the associated safety questions.
Additionally, the work is expected to be completed prior to the completion of the construction of
LMGS, in alignment with 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) requirements. Therefore, the NRC staff
determined that the R&D activities planned for SR metallic SSCs are consistent with the
requirements of 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) and 10 CFR 50.35(a)(3).

Fuel

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 13.3.3, which includes Xe-100 fuel as part of the LMGS
R&D program to confirm acceptable burnup, fast fluence, and temperature limits planned for the
operation of Xe-100. The planned testing is to confirm the gaps in safety testing to ensure that
the burnup, fast fluence, and temperature limits outside the validated range for these
parameters will not challenge the TRISO fuel particles and pebbles to perform its RSF. The
PSAR states X-energy Pebble Reactor Test (XPeRT) irradiation testing is planned, as described
in PSAR section 6.4.2.3, to demonstrate performance of the Xe-100 fuel.

The NRC staff reviewed the fuel qualification methodology elements discussed in PSAR
section 6.4.2.3 and finds that the elements include the confirmation of gaps in the safety testing
to validate burnup, fast fluence, and temperature ranges for the Xe-100 fuel. Specifically, the
testing program supports the evaluation models to conservatively predict fission product release
from fuel pebbles under operating and licensing basis event conditions.

The NRC staff notes that preliminary peak fuel temperatures for the limiting DBA analyzed in
PSAR section 3.6, are beyond the limits typically associated with TRISO fuel particles, including
the results from the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Gas Reactor (AGR) program. A
survey of literature and testing data available for TRISO fuel (“TRISO Fuel: Properties and
Failure Modes,” ML21175A1522) generally indicates that modern TRISO fuel demonstrates
robustness through 1600 degrees Celsius (°C) (2912 degrees Fahrenheit (°F)), with 1800°C

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


(3272°F) generally being best characterized as the severe accident temperature. The NRC staff
finds that planned testing to specifically qualify the fuel for temperatures expected during LBEs
for Xe-100, including accounting for uncertainties, is an essential step to resolving safety
questions pertaining to retention of fission products in fuel particles and pebbles, and overall
release.

Because LME’s planned testing addresses burnup, fast fluence, and temperature ranges for the
Xe-100 fuel, the NRC staff determined that the planned testing will reasonably resolve the
associated safety questions. Additionally, the work is expected to be completed prior to the
completion of the construction of LMGS, in alignment with 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) requirements.
Therefore, the NRC staff determined that the R&D activities planned for the fuel qualification
methodology are consistent with the requirements of 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) and 10 CFR
50.35(a)(3).

13.2.   Conclusion

The NRC staff finds that LME meets the requirements of 10 CFR 50.34(a)(8) because LME has:
(1) identified the SSCs that require research and development to confirm the adequacy of the
design, (2) identified and described the R&D program which will be conducted to resolve any
safety questions associated with such SSCs, and (3) has provided a commitment that these
safety questions will be resolved prior to completion of construction of the LMGS.

Based on these considerations, the NRC staff determined that the discussion presented in the
R&D program is sufficient to support issuance of a CP pursuant to the requirements of 10 CFR
50.35(a)(3).
